question: What type(s) of USCG-approved personal flotation device (PFD) must Georgia vessels carry for each person on board?
choice_b: A single PFD regardless of the number of passengers
choice_c: At least one USCG-approved Type I, II, III, or V PFD for each person on board
choice_d: Only a Type IV throwable cushion for each passenger
explanation: All Georgia vessels must have at least one USCG-approved Type I, II, III, or V PFD for each person on board; Type V PFDs are acceptable only when worn and securely fastened.
source_note: Handbook of Georgia Boating Laws and Responsibilities, 'Personal Flotation Devices (PFDs)'

question: Besides wearable PFDs, what additional device must most boats carry on board and readily accessible?
choice_a: A spare anchor for every passenger
choice_c: An extra set of oars for every PFD on board
choice_d: One USCG-approved throwable device (except on vessels less than 16 feet long, including PWC, canoes, and kayaks)
explanation: In addition to wearable PFDs, one USCG-approved throwable device must be on board and readily accessible on all boats except those less than 16 feet long, including PWC, canoes, and kayaks.
source_note: Handbook of Georgia Boating Laws and Responsibilities, 'Personal Flotation Devices (PFDs)'

question: Under Georgia law, when must a child under 13 years of age wear a USCG-approved PFD?
choice_a: While on board any moving vessel, unless the child is in a fully enclosed cabin
choice_b: Only when the child cannot swim
choice_c: Only on vessels longer than 26 feet
choice_d: Only when the vessel is anchored
explanation: Georgia law requires all children under 13 years of age to wear a USCG-approved PFD while on board any moving vessel; this requirement does not apply when the child is in a fully enclosed cabin.
source_note: Handbook of Georgia Boating Laws and Responsibilities, 'Personal Flotation Devices (PFDs)'

question: What PFD requirement applies to every person riding on a personal watercraft (PWC) in Georgia?
choice_a: PFDs are optional if the rider is a strong swimmer
choice_b: Each person must wear a USCG-approved Type I, II, III, or V PFD that is properly fitted and fastened; inflatable PFDs are not approved for PWC use
choice_c: Only the operator, not passengers, must wear a PFD
choice_d: Any flotation cushion carried on board satisfies the requirement
explanation: Each person riding a PWC must wear a properly fitted and fastened USCG-approved Type I, II, III, or V PFD; inflatable PFDs are specifically not approved for PWC use.
source_note: Handbook of Georgia Boating Laws and Responsibilities, 'Personal Flotation Devices (PFDs)'

question: What must a person being towed on water skis or a similar device wear in Georgia?
choice_a: No flotation device is required if the person is an experienced skier
choice_c: A ski belt, ski jacket, or Type I, II, or III PFD that is properly fitted and fastened
choice_d: A Type IV throwable cushion held under one arm
explanation: Persons being towed on water skis or a similar device must wear a ski belt, ski jacket, or a Type I, II, or III PFD that is properly fitted and fastened.
source_note: Handbook of Georgia Boating Laws and Responsibilities, 'Personal Flotation Devices (PFDs)'

question: What does the numeric 'performance level' icon (typically 50 to 150) on newer-style PFD labels indicate?
choice_a: The exact retail price of the PFD
choice_b: The number of years the PFD remains under warranty
choice_c: The maximum number of people the single PFD can support at once
choice_d: A lower number is intended for near-shore activities in calm water with greater mobility and comfort, while a higher number is intended for offshore use with greater flotation and turning ability
explanation: New-style PFD labels use a performance level number: lower numbers suit near-shore, calm-water use with more mobility, while higher numbers suit offshore use with greater flotation, turning ability, and stability.
source_note: Handbook of Georgia Boating Laws and Responsibilities, 'PFD Label'

question: Under what condition may a Type V PFD be substituted for another required PFD type in Georgia?
choice_a: Only if it is specifically approved by the USCG for the activity at hand, and it may not be substituted on children weighing less than 90 pounds
choice_b: Any Type V PFD may always be substituted for any other type with no restriction
choice_c: Type V PFDs may never be substituted under any circumstance
choice_d: Type V PFDs may only be used by adults over 200 pounds
explanation: A Type V PFD may substitute for another required type only if it is specifically USCG-approved for the activity at hand; it may not be substituted for children weighing less than 90 pounds.
source_note: Handbook of Georgia Boating Laws and Responsibilities, 'Personal Flotation Devices (PFDs)'

question: What condition must all PFDs on board a Georgia vessel meet?
choice_a: They must all be the exact same size
choice_b: They must be in good and serviceable condition and readily accessible
choice_c: They must be stored in a locked compartment at all times
choice_d: They must be replaced every boating season regardless of condition
explanation: All PFDs carried on board must be in good and serviceable condition and must be readily accessible to the people who may need them.
source_note: Handbook of Georgia Boating Laws and Responsibilities, 'Personal Flotation Devices (PFDs)'

question: What is true about the 'turn ability' feature described on a USCG-approved PFD label?
choice_a: All PFDs automatically turn a wearer face up regardless of the label
choice_b: Turn ability refers to how easily the PFD can be put on, not how it performs in water
choice_c: A PFD marked with turn ability will turn an unconscious person face up, while one without it will not
choice_d: Turn ability only applies to Type IV throwable devices
explanation: PFD labels indicate turn ability: some PFDs are designed to turn an unconscious person face up, while others will not, which is an important safety distinction to check before use.
source_note: Handbook of Georgia Boating Laws and Responsibilities, 'PFD Label'

question: If a boater chooses to wear a PFD that is not USCG approved, what must still be carried on board in Georgia?
choice_b: A written waiver signed by all passengers
choice_c: A second non-approved PFD as a backup
choice_d: A properly fitting USCG-approved PFD, to meet state and federal carriage requirements
explanation: If a person chooses to wear a non-USCG-approved PFD when one is not specifically required, a properly fitting USCG-approved PFD must still be carried on board to meet state and federal carriage requirements.
source_note: Handbook of Georgia Boating Laws and Responsibilities, 'Personal Flotation Devices (PFDs)'
